name: Argument Coherence Analysis
description: Evaluates logical coherence and flow of argumentation structures — AI often produces superficially coherent but logically weak arguments.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated text by analyzing the logical structure and coherence of arguments. AI text often reads fluently but, when analyzed structurally, reveals shallow reasoning and weak logical connections:

1. **Argument Mining and Graph Construction**: The method identifies argumentative components using a BERT-based argument mining model: claims (propositions being argued for), premises (supporting evidence or reasoning), and conclusions. These components are linked by argumentative relations: support (premise offers evidence for claim), attack (premise contradicts claim), and rebuttal (counterargument). The resulting argument graph represents the text's logical structure. For each argument, the method computes: (a) argument depth — maximum chain length from evidence to conclusion (human text: 2–4 levels; AI text: 1–2 levels), (b) argument breadth — number of independent premises supporting each claim (human: 2–5; AI: 1–2 with repetition), (c) graph connectivity — ratio of edges to nodes (human: 1.5–2.5; AI: 0.8–1.2). AI text tends to produce flat, linear argument structures rather than the multi-layered reasoning found in human writing.

2. **Logical Validity Checking**: The method evaluates logical connections between premises and conclusions using natural language inference (NLI). For each premise-conclusion pair, NLI classifies the relationship as: entailment (premise logically supports conclusion), contradiction (premise undermines conclusion), or neutral (no logical connection). Human arguments show 60–75% entailment between linked premise-conclusion pairs. AI text shows two failure modes: (a) pseudo-coherence — premises use thematically related vocabulary but have neutral logical connection to conclusions (40–55% neutral despite appearing connected), (b) circular reasoning — the conclusion essentially restates the premise in different words (detectable via high semantic similarity > 0.85 between premise and conclusion embeddings). The method flags arguments where NLI entailment < 50% or where premise-conclusion similarity > 0.80.

3. **Evidence Specificity and Grounding**: Human arguments are grounded in specific evidence: statistics, examples, citations, personal experience, or expert testimony. The method classifies evidence types and measures: (a) evidence specificity — human text provides precise details (dates, numbers, names); AI text provides vague or generic evidence ("studies show", "research suggests", "many experts agree"), (b) evidence relevance — the semantic distance between evidence and claim (human: cosine > 0.5; AI evidence is often tangentially related), (c) evidence verifiability — whether cited facts can be checked (human text references verifiable events; AI text references plausible-sounding but unverifiable claims). The specificity score uses named entity density, numeral density, and hedging word frequency to produce a composite score (human: > 0.6; AI: < 0.4 on 0–1 scale).

4. **Counterargument and Concession Patterns**: Mature argumentation addresses opposing viewpoints through concession and rebuttal. The method checks: (a) counterargument presence — human argumentative text includes 1–3 counterarguments per 1000 words; AI text either omits counterarguments entirely or adds a token counterargument in a formulaic pattern ("While some may argue..., however..."), (b) concession depth — human writers genuinely engage with opposing views, showing semantic shift between concession and rebuttal; AI concessions are shallow (the rebuttal simply repeats the original claim), measured by the semantic distance between concession and subsequent rebuttal (human: cosine < 0.6; AI: cosine > 0.75), (c) argument progression — human arguments build cumulatively, with later paragraphs referencing earlier evidence; AI arguments tend to be modular (each paragraph is self-contained, not referencing previous paragraphs).
parameters:
Argument mining model: BERT-based (ArgMin)
Argument depth human: 2–4 levels
Argument depth AI: 1–2 levels
NLI entailment threshold: > 50%
Circular reasoning threshold: cosine > 0.80
Evidence specificity human: > 0.6
Evidence specificity AI: < 0.4
Concession depth threshold: cosine < 0.6
Counterargument density: 1–3 per 1000 words
Minimum text length: 300 words
accuracy: 79–88% accuracy detecting AI-generated argumentative text. Argument graph structure achieves AUC of 0.85. NLI-based validity checking provides F1-score of 0.83. Evidence specificity adds 4–6% improvement. Performance best for persuasive essays and op-eds, lower for narrative or descriptive text.
source: Stab, C. & Gurevych, I. (2017). Parsing Argumentation Structures in Persuasive Essays. Computational Linguistics, 43(3), 619–659.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated persuasive essays and opinion articles. Academic integrity checking for argumentative writing. Evaluating argument quality in debate and policy analysis. Identifying AI-written editorials and commentary.
strengths:
• Targets logical reasoning depth — a fundamental weakness of current AI
• Argument graph structure captures organization beyond surface fluency
• NLI-based validity checking detects pseudo-coherent arguments
• Evidence specificity measures real-world grounding
• Counterargument analysis assesses intellectual engagement
limitations:
• Argument mining accuracy limits downstream analysis quality
• Descriptive and narrative text has different argumentation patterns
• Some human writers also produce weak arguments
• Requires sufficient argumentative content (not effective on informational text)
• Advanced AI models are improving at structured argumentation

references.title: Stab, C. & Gurevych, I. — Parsing Argumentation Structures in Persuasive Essays (Computational Linguistics 2017)
Liu, Z. et al. — Argument Mining: A Survey (ACL 2022)
Walton, D. — Argumentation Schemes for AI and Law (Argument & Computation 2019)
